extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of English literature; literary critics; poets and scholars interested in poetic style and comparative literature
extracted.subtask_description: Critical criteria for evaluating poetry's characteristic qualities (style, melancholy, and natural magic) and the modes of handling nature, with comparative examples across Celtic, English, German, Greek, and Latin traditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Turn for style (power of style)
rubrics_metrics.description: A national/poetical 'turn for style'—a peculiar recasting and heightening of language under spiritual excitement which adds dignity and distinction to expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinct from plain idiomatic or nervous expression; manifested as intensified, bridled excitement in delivery (examples: Dante, Milton, Pindar, Cicero, Bossuet, Bolingbroke). Compare Milton passage with Goethe to see the heightened poetical style. Style's characteristic effect is to 'add dignity and distinction.' Evaluate passages for this 'kneading, heightening, and recasting' produced by emotional pressure; absence of such heightened manner indicates lack of this turn for style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Turn for melancholy / Titanism
rubrics_metrics.description: A strain of passionate, turbulent, indomitable melancholy (Titanism) in poetry — a vehement reaction against the despotism of fact and an intense, struggling longing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attribute often linked to Celtic sources; contrast with German 'Sehnsucht' (wistful, soft longing) as in Werther. Examples: Llywarch Hen, Macpherson's Ossian, Byron (Manfred, Lara, Cain), Milton's Satan passages. When assessing a poem, look for fervent, defiant, self-consuming revolt and passionate personal anguish rather than calmly explained motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Turn for natural magic (the Celtic gift)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'magical' intimacy with nature: an interpretation that renders nature's intimate life, fairy charm, and weird power rather than mere beauty or realism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not simply faithful description or classical radiance but a 'magically vivid and near interpretation' (examples: Celtic romances' flower-made maidens, Peredur's snow/raven imagery, Shakespeare's fairy-dew passages, Keats's 'magic casements'). This quality requires fine handling; imitations by other literatures may lack the native 'stamp of perfectness.' Evaluate diction, imagery, and the sense of nature's secret life to judge presence of natural magic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventional way of handling nature
rubrics_metrics.description: A mode where the eye is not on the object; nature is treated by conventional, formulaic phrases (e.g., eighteenth-century poetic clichés).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: clichéd openings like 'As when the moon, refulgent lamp of night--' and many Latin poetic conceits. Identification of conventional handling is an anti-pattern: look for generic, recycled images and lack of direct attention to the observed object.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faithful way of handling nature
rubrics_metrics.description: A mode in which the eye is on the object and gives a straightforward, faithful depiction without added radiancy or magic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common in German poetry (example: Goethe's Zueignung stanzas). Valuable for moral or spiritual emotion but lacking Greek brightness or Celtic magic. When evaluating, note accuracy and fidelity of description but also whether the work adds higher-level luminous or magical qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greek way of handling nature
rubrics_metrics.description: A mode where the eye is on the object but radiancy and brightness are added—classical clarity and luminousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Homer, Theocritus, Virgil, and Keats's 'What little town by river or seashore...' Characterized by clear, bright composition; assess for luminous imagery, classical balance, and added radiance beyond mere faithful depiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magical way of handling nature
rubrics_metrics.description: A mode where the eye is on the object but charm and magic are added, producing fairy-like, intimate, and uncanny renderings of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the Celtic mode of 'natural magic' illustrated in Celtic romance and in passages from Keats and Shakespeare (e.g., Peredur's snow/raven/blood simile, Geraint and Enid's river and tree scenes). Evaluate for closeness, specificity, wonder, and an animating of natural elements into secret life; judge whether the handling attains magical clearness and nearness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetical simplicity vs prose simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea that 'simplicity' in great poetry is a poetical simplicity—the result of a heightened manner—not the plain simplicity of prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: simple passages in Pindar, Dante, Shakespeare are 'masterpieces of poetical simplicity'—they are the crowning moments of a manner pitched differently from prose. When assessing 'simplicity' in verse, determine whether simplicity arises from refined poetical shaping rather than ordinary prose plainness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between idiomatic expression and elevated style
rubrics_metrics.description: Power of idiomatic, simple, nervous, racy expression (e.g., Luther, Cobbett) is not the same as the elevated 'power of style' that imparts dignity and distinction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate forceful colloquial or idiomatic diction with the recast, heightened manner that constitutes true 'style' in the essay's sense. Use examples (Luther, Cobbett vs Dante, Milton) to test whether energy of language is idiomatic robustness or an artistic, dignifying stylistic transformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity and native stamp versus imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: When a nation borrows an aptitude (e.g., natural magic), imitation across literatures can occur but lacks the 'stamp of perfectness' that marks the gift where it is native.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious when attributing a poetic quality to a tradition: check whether the effect shows native perfection (as in Celtic originals) or a derivative, less complete imitation (as in later German or other borrowings). This affects judgments of originality and depth of the poetic effect.
